summary.text: Fertilization is the fusion of gametes to give rise to a zygote and start its development into a new individual organism.
The cycle of fertilization and development of new individuals is called sexual reproduction, and pollination or insemination, which come before gametes fuse, are technically separate processes.
In flowering plants, double fertilization has one sperm fuse with the egg to form a zygote and the other join two polar nuclei to form a triploid cell that becomes the endosperm.

items.prompt: A bee drops pollen onto a flower's stigma. Has fertilization happened yet?

options.label: Yes, because pollination and fertilization are the same event
Yes, but only in flowers that make several seeds
No, because the gametes have not yet fused
No, because it only ever happens in animals

items.explain: Pollination comes before the fusion of gametes, so the two are separate processes; fertilization occurs when a sperm fuses with the egg.

items.prompt: The sperm of most seed plants cannot move on their own. How does one reach the egg?

options.label: A growing pollen tube carries it to the ovule
It swims through fluid in the style
Wind blows it directly into the ovule
Insects carry it straight into the embryo sac

items.explain: Unlike motile animal sperm, seed plant sperm relies on the pollen tube to carry it to the ovule, where it is released.

items.prompt: In a flowering plant, one sperm cell fuses with the egg. What happens to the other sperm cell?

options.label: It also fuses with the egg, making a second zygote
It breaks down together with the egg cell
It waits in reserve for a later pollination
It fuses with two polar nuclei, forming a triploid cell

items.explain: The second sperm fuses with the two polar nuclei, and the resulting triploid cell divides to form the endosperm.

items.prompt: Experiments on frogs in the late 1700s showed what was needed to form a zygote. What was it?

options.label: Warm water surrounding the eggs
Interaction between ovum and sperm
The ovum acting on its own
The sperm acting on its own

items.explain: Spallanzani established that interaction between the female's ovum and the male's sperm is needed to form a zygote in frogs.

items.prompt: In the plant Arabidopsis, what directly makes a pollen tube burst and release its sperm?

options.label: Enzymes digesting the wall of the ovule
Pressure from the swelling of the ovary
A surge of calcium uptake from open channels
Loss of the tube's nuclei before arrival

items.explain: Reactive oxygen species made under control of ovule proteins activate calcium channels, and the large calcium uptake ruptures the tube.

items.prompt: A fruit holds many seeds, each formed from its own ovule. What does this imply about pollination?

options.label: Many pollen grains are needed, one for each ovule
One pollen grain fertilizes every ovule at once
Pollen is not needed once the first seed forms
Only the sperm of other flowers can fertilize extra ovules

items.explain: With multi-seeded fruits, multiple grains of pollen are necessary for syngamy with each ovule.

paragraphs.heading: Two cells become one
paragraphs.text: Fertilization, also called syngamy, is the fusion of two gametes into a single new cell, the zygote. That zygote then starts to grow into a new organism. Steps that come before the fusion, such as insemination or pollination, are sometimes loosely called fertilization too, but strictly speaking they are separate events. The repeating cycle of fertilization followed by the growth of new individuals is what biologists call sexual reproduction.

paragraphs.heading: How the idea took shape
paragraphs.text: In ancient times Aristotle pictured new individuals forming when male and female fluids merged, with shape and function appearing bit by bit, a pattern he called epigenetic. In 1784 Spallanzani showed, working with frogs, that an egg and a sperm have to interact before a zygote can form. In 1827 Karl Ernst von Baer became the first to see the egg of a therian mammal. In 1876 Oscar Hertwig, in Germany, described the nuclei of sea urchin sperm and eggs fusing together.

paragraphs.heading: Deep roots
paragraphs.text: The way fertilization evolved is tied to the origin of meiosis, since both are parts of sexual reproduction, which arose in eukaryotes. One hypothesis holds that meiosis grew out of mitosis.

paragraphs.heading: Fertilization in plants
paragraphs.text: In plants the two gametes are the sperm, which is male, and the egg cell, which is female, but different plant groups bring them together in different ways. In bryophytes and pteridophytes, sperm and egg meet inside the archegonium. In seed plants, the male gametophyte develops within a pollen grain. After pollination the grain germinates and grows a pollen tube, which enters the ovule through a tiny pore called the micropyle. Unlike animal sperm, which can move, the sperm of most seed plants cannot, and it relies on the tube to carry it to the ovule.

paragraphs.heading: Guiding and bursting the tube
paragraphs.text: Work on tobacco plants found a family of glycoproteins, called TTS proteins, that boost pollen tube growth. Tubes grew three times as fast in a medium containing them as in a sugar-free one, and tubes stretched toward the proteins when they were placed on pistils. Plants that could not make TTS proteins had slower tube growth and lower fertility. In Arabidopsis, the tube breaks open only after a signal from the female gametophyte: proteins in the ovule called FER protein kinases control the making of reactive oxygen species (ROS), very reactive forms of oxygen. High ROS levels open calcium channels in the tube, calcium floods in, and the tube ruptures and lets out its sperm.

paragraphs.heading: Double fertilization
paragraphs.text: Flowering plants, the angiosperms, use double fertilization: the two sperm from a pollen tube fertilize two different cells inside the female gametophyte, also known as the embryo sac, which sits within an ovule. One sperm joins the egg cell and makes a diploid (2n) zygote. The nucleus of the other sperm fuses with two haploid polar nuclei in the central cell, giving a triploid (3n) cell. That cell divides by mitosis to build the endosperm, a tissue rich in nutrients, inside the seed. Once fertilized, the ovary begins to swell and turns into the fruit.
